ML-systems design: the 45-minute method and the numbers

This chapter and the next three are imported from the companion RL Infra System Design playbook: how to answer an ML-systems design question about RL infrastructure, inference or training in 45 minutes. It assumes the algorithms from Part IV (GRPO, PPO, inference) and teaches the systems around them. Links marked “Field Guide §n” go to the companion RL Infrastructure Field Guide.

Plain wordsA kitchen that cooks, tastes and learns

RL training is a kitchen where cooks (the rollout fleet) try recipes, tasters (reward services) score each dish, and a head chef (the trainer) rewrites the recipe book after every round and hands new copies to every cook (weight sync). Every design question is the same kitchen at a different size: how many cooks, how many tasters, how long the slowest dish takes, and how fast you can hand out new recipe books.

The method: ask a few questions that change the kitchen, do the arithmetic, draw the kitchen, then dig into the part the arithmetic says will break.

For leadersWhat a strong answer shows

Scoping that finds the two or three answers that change the architecture; numbers that choose between designs rather than decorate them; a complete end-to-end design; depth on the real bottleneck; failure handling and cost raised before the interviewer asks; and a path from v1 to v3. Managers add teams, staffing and risk. The worked plan below (a 70B coding agent on 1,024 H100s) is the reference every later problem resizes.

TL;DR

  • Run the round in six stages: requirements (5 min), numbers (5), the design (10), two or three deep dives (15), failures and scale (7), recap (3). The first ten minutes decide the design. §1
  • Every prompt is the same machine at a different size: a rollout fleet, sandboxed environments, reward services, a trainer and a weight-sync path, joined by an orchestrator, and built today from vLLM, FSDP2, a Ray driver and Docker containers on Kubernetes or Slurm. The requirements decide which part is the bottleneck. §2 §3 §5
  • Do the token accounting first. The trainer runs forward and backward over every token in the context; decode produces only the model's own tokens, at about HBM bandwidth ÷ (KV bytes × context) per GPU. A 70B coding agent on 1,024 H100s needs about 300 rollout and 720 trainer GPUs, takes a 13-minute step and keeps about 7,000 sandboxes alive. §4
  • Agentic RL runs asynchronously. A synchronous step waits for the slowest trajectory and then trains (33 minutes here, against 13 asynchronous), so the fleet keeps generating and takes new weights mid-flight: vLLM's pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=False) plus a weight-transfer engine, version tags on tokens, staleness capped at four steps, and importance-sampling correction. §5 §11
  • Failures grow with GPU count. Llama 3 saw about one interruption per 2,100 GPU-days, so a 4,096-GPU job is interrupted about twice a day. Losing a rollout replica costs minutes; losing a trainer rank costs the step, so checkpoint the trainer asynchronously about every √(2 × save cost × MTBF). §10 §12
  • Weight sync is a data-movement problem. A 1T model in BF16 takes about 52 s to broadcast through one link at 40 GB/s (about 20 s in FP8 at line rate), against 1–7 s as sharded FP8 point-to-point copies (Perplexity reports 1.3 s; open-source stacks 4–7 s). §9 §13

§01

The 45-minute arc

What does a strong ML-systems design answer look like in 45 minutes, and what do interviewers score at senior, staff and manager level?

Six stages with time boxes: requirements (0–5 min), numbers (5–10), the high-level design (10–20), two or three deep dives chosen by the numbers (20–35), failures, scale and evolution (35–42), and a recap (42–45). The same six signals are scored at every level: scoping, estimation, design, depth, operations and evolution. What changes with level is how much you drive the trade-offs yourself and, for managers, how the design maps onto teams, plans and risk.

1 · Requirements2 · Numbers3 · Design4 · Deep dives5 · Failures6
0 min510203542

  1. 1 · 0–5 min

    Requirements

    On the board: the goal in one line, five to eight requirements with numbers, and your stated assumptions.

    Say: “Before I draw anything, let me pin down what we're training, on what hardware, and what good looks like.”

  2. 2 · 5–10 min

    Numbers

    On the board: tokens per step, GPU-hours for rollout and training, the GPU split, concurrency, bytes per weight sync.

    Say: “Let me size it first. The numbers will tell us where the bottleneck is.”

  3. 3 · 10–20 min

    The design

    On the board: the reference diagram from §2, adapted, with every arrow labelled with what flows and how often.

    Say: “Here is the path of one trajectory, and then the path of one weight update.”

  4. 4 · 20–35 min

    Deep dives

    On the board: the two or three bottlenecks the numbers exposed, each with options, a choice, and the API that implements it.

    Say: “The two hard parts are asynchrony and the sandbox fleet. Which would you like first?”

  5. 5 · 35–42 min

    Failures and scale

    On the board: what fails, how you detect it and how you recover; what changes at ten times the scale; how you roll changes out.

    Say: “Here is what pages someone at 3 am, and how the system heals without them.”

  6. 6 · 42–45 min

    Recap

    On the board: four sentences: the design, the three key numbers, the biggest risk, and what you would build first.

    Say: “To summarize: …” Then stop and ask what they would push on.

Lead the conversation. Check in at each stage boundary (“does this match what you had in mind?”), follow the interviewer when they redirect, and when they go quiet, take the bottleneck your numbers point at. Keep one corner of the board for numbers and assumptions and keep pointing back at it; it is the evidence for every choice you make later.

What is scored, by level

This is how these rounds are commonly described in public, not any one company's rubric.

Five ways to lose the round

  1. Drawing boxes before you have numbers, so nothing in the design is justified.
  2. Naming technologies without saying what each one does in this design (“we use Ray” is not an answer; “Ray actors own the engines so one driver can pause all of them” is).
  3. Spending ten minutes on a component nobody asked about.
  4. Leaving failures and cost until the interviewer raises them.
  5. Never committing. Every trade-off ends in a choice and the condition that would change it.

§02

The reference design

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

What machine sits behind almost every RL-infrastructure prompt, and which four mechanisms decide its shape?

Six parts: an orchestrator, a rollout fleet of inference engines, environments running in sandboxes, reward services, a trainer and a weight-sync path, with storage and a control plane around them. Four forces decide their shape: the long tail of trajectory lengths, staleness and its importance-sampling correction, train–inference mismatch, and the cost of moving weights. Every worked problem in Part 3 is this picture at a different size.

The nouns in this picturevLLM is the inference engine. A replica is one copy of the model on a few GPUs, split by tensor parallelism (TP: every weight matrix cut across one node's GPUs) or, for MoE, by data-parallel attention plus expert parallelism (DP+EP). FSDP2 is PyTorch's sharded trainer and DCP its checkpoint format. NCCL is NVIDIA's library for collectives between GPUs, and NIXL its library for point-to-point transfers between GPUs over RDMA; CUDA IPC lets two processes on one machine share GPU memory; RDMA lets a network card read or write another machine's GPU memory without either CPU. Ray lets one driver program start and call processes across the cluster. A Docker container is an isolated process started from an image; runc, gVisor and microVMs are the runtimes that start it, from weakest isolation to strongest. Kubernetes and Slurm are cluster schedulers, and a gang is a job whose processes must all start together. Egress is outbound network traffic. Part 2 builds each one.

One trajectory, start to finish

  1. The orchestrator takes a task from the task queue and asks the environment service for a sandbox with the task's image (§8).
  2. It sends the prompt's token IDs to a rollout engine, which samples tokens and returns them with their log-probabilities; the orchestrator tags each span of tokens with the weight version that was live, starting a new span at each pause (§5).
  3. Each tool call runs in the sandbox; the observation is tokenized and appended to the context. This repeats until the episode ends or hits its turn or token cap.
  4. The reward service scores the finished trajectory, or marks it void if the infrastructure failed (§8).
  5. The trajectory waits in the buffer until all G samples of its task are done; complete groups become training batches (§7).
  6. The trainer recomputes log-probabilities, applies the loss with importance weights and steps the optimizer (§6).
  7. The weight-sync path ships the new weights to every engine and bumps the version (§9). The control plane schedules all of it and restarts whatever fails (§10).

The four forces

Each force is derived in the Field Guide; here is what each one does to the design.

  • The long tail

    sets wall-clock time

    Generation time is the larger of work ÷ throughput and slowest trajectory ÷ per-sequence speed. Agent trajectories vary several-fold in length, so a synchronous step mostly waits for a few stragglers. The consequence is asynchronous pools (§11). Field Guide §1

  • Staleness

    sets what the trainer must correct

    When weights change during generation, samples come from an older policy μ. Correct with per-token truncated importance weights (TIS, decoupled PPO, CISPO) and cap the age at K steps; raw sequence-level weights collapse on long trajectories (GSPO and TOPR survive by length-normalizing or truncating the ratio). The consequence is version tags on tokens and a staleness filter (§7). Field Guide §6

  • Train–inference mismatch

    sets what the engine must return

    With identical weights, the engine and the trainer still compute different probabilities (kernels, FP8, batch order, MoE routing). Measure it with the k3 KL estimator on the same tokens and fix it cheapest first: truncated IS, an FP32 LM head, routing replay for MoE, sampling masks, batch-invariant kernels. The consequence is the API list in §5. Field Guide §7

  • Sync cost

    sets the transport

    Every step moves the whole model: about S ÷ b through one link, or about S ÷ (g·b) when each engine GPU pulls only its own shard. A 70B model in BF16 broadcasts in about 3.5 s; a 1T model in about 52 s, against 1–7 s sharded (Perplexity 1.3 s). The consequence is the transport choice in §9. Field Guide §8

§03

Requirements that change the design

Which clarifying questions actually change the architecture, and what does each answer do to it?

Ten questions, each tied to one design decision: model size and architecture (replica size, expert parallelism, sync transport), episode shape (sandboxes, asynchrony, KV pressure), reward source (verifier fleet or judge fleet), freshness (synchronous or bounded staleness), cluster (colocated or split, scheduler), throughput target (batch per step), tenancy (platform or single loop), determinism, execution safety (isolation tier) and budget. Ask the five that matter most, then state assumptions for the rest.

QuestionIf the answer is……the design does this
Model size and type8–70B dense / 200B–1T MoEDense: TP inside a node, FSDP2 trainer, NCCL broadcast is fine. MoE: DP+EP engines of 16–64 GPUs, an EP trainer (Megatron or TorchTitan), sharded weight sync, routing replay.
Episode shapeOne answer / a multi-turn agent with toolsSingle-turn: one generate call per sample, groups of G via n=G. Agent: sandboxes, token-in/token-out, sticky routing for prefix-cache hits, asynchronous pools, KV offload.
Reward sourceUnit tests / an LLM judge / human preferenceTests: a CPU verifier fleet next to the sandboxes. Judge: a GPU judge service with caching and versioned rubrics (§15). Preference: a reward model served like a judge.
FreshnessStrictly on-policy / a few steps of lag is fineStrict: synchronous colocated loop, accept idle GPUs. Lag allowed: asynchronous split pools with max staleness K and IS correction.
ClusterDedicated or shared; how many GPUs, which interconnectSmall or shared: colocate with sleep/wake. Large and dedicated: split pools. Shared: a queueing scheduler with gang admission and preemption (§10).
Throughput targetSteps per day or tokens per daySets the batch per step and therefore the fleet sizes through the formulas in §4.
TenancyOne research loop / ten teamsOne loop: optimize the loop. Ten teams: quotas, shared services, standard interfaces, correctness gates (§14).
DeterminismBitwise reruns needed / statistical reproducibility is enoughBitwise: batch-invariant kernels, fixed seeds and data order, pinned versions; costs throughput. Otherwise: version everything and log enough to replay.
Execution safetyTrusted code / arbitrary model-written codeEither way, a Docker container per trajectory on its own CPU nodes. For model-written code, block network egress except to package mirrors and set hard resource limits; choose the runtime by what else shares the nodes: plain runc on dedicated nodes, gVisor or a microVM otherwise (§8).
Budget and deadlineFixed GPUs and weeks / open-endedFixed: buy before build (verl, SkyRL, prime-rl, NeMo-RL) and cut scope. Open-ended: build the parts that differentiate.
Say it

“Before I draw, five questions. What model, dense or MoE, and how big? What does an episode look like, one answer or an agent with tools, and how long? Where does the reward come from? How fresh must samples be? And what hardware do we have, and is it ours? Unless you say otherwise I'll assume a 70B dense model, coding tasks with up to 50 tool calls and unit-test rewards, up to four steps of lag, and 1,024 H100s that we own.”

§04

Numbers: the estimation toolkit

Which numbers size an RL system, and how do you produce them in five minutes?

A few hardware constants (H100: 989 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s of HBM, the GPU's own memory, 80 GB, about 50 GB/s per network card or NIC), six formulas (trainer FLOPs per token, KV bytes per token, decode speed, Little's law, sync time, failure interval) and a fixed order to apply them. For a 70B coding agent on 1,024 H100s they give about 300 rollout and 720 trainer GPUs, a 13-minute step, 11-minute trajectories and 7,100 sandboxes in flight. The planner below runs the same arithmetic for any setup.

Constants to carry

GPUBF16 denseFP8 denseHBMHBM bandwidthNVLink, per directionNetwork, per GPU
H100 SXM989 TFLOP/s1,979 TFLOP/s80 GB3.35 TB/s450 GB/s400 Gb/s ≈ 50 GB/s
H200989 TFLOP/s1,979 TFLOP/s141 GB4.8 TB/s450 GB/s≈ 50 GB/s
B2002,250 TFLOP/s4,500 TFLOP/s180 GB8 TB/s900 GB/s≈ 50–100 GB/s

Real systems reach a fraction of peak: 30–40% MFU (model FLOPs utilization, the share of peak FLOP/s spent on the model's own math) for dense training and 20–30% for MoE, 50–70% of HBM bandwidth in decode, about 80% of NIC line rate. Three more numbers come up constantly: PCIe Gen5 x16 moves about 64 GB/s each way, a SWE-style task image is 1–2.5 GB, and Llama 3's pre-training saw one unexpected interruption per about 2,100 GPU-days.

Six formulas

1 · Trainer FLOPs per token

\[C_{\text{train}} \approx (3 + r)\,\big(2N_{\text{act}} + 2\,n_{\text{layer}}\,L\,d_{\text{attn}}\big)\]

Forward and backward cost three forward passes; \(r = 1\) adds the forward pass that recomputes the old policy's log-probs. The second term is causal attention over a sequence of \(L\) tokens, and at 32K tokens it adds 30% to a 70B model's \(2N\). Divide by MFU × peak: a 70B at 35% MFU spends about 2.1 ms of H100 time per training token. MFU counts the model's own FLOPs only, so the 35% already absorbs the extra forward pass of activation checkpointing (§6).

2 · KV-cache bytes per token

\[\text{kv}_{\text{GQA}} = 2\,n_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{kv}}\,d_{\text{head}}\times\text{bytes}\]
\[\text{kv}_{\text{MLA}} = n_{\text{layer}}\,(d_c + d_{\text{rope}})\times\text{bytes}\]

A 70B with 80 layers and 8 KV heads of 128 dimensions holds 320 KiB per token in BF16 and 160 KiB in FP8, so one 32K-token trajectory pins 5.2 GB of FP8 cache. DeepSeek-style MLA, multi-head latent attention, which caches one small compressed vector per token and layer instead of full keys and values (61 layers, 512 + 64 dimensions) needs 69 KiB per token in BF16.

3 · Decode speed

\[t_{\text{step}} \approx \frac{W + m\,\text{kv}\,\bar L}{g\,\eta\,\text{BW}}\]
\[\frac{\text{tokens/s}}{\text{GPU}} = \frac{m}{g\,t_{\text{step}}} \;\le\; \frac{\eta\,\text{BW}}{\text{kv}\,\bar L}\]

Each engine step, one forward pass that advances every running sequence by a token, reads the weights \(W\) once and the KV cache of every one of the \(m\) running sequences, spread over the replica's \(g\) GPUs. At a long average context \(\bar L\) the second term dominates and batching stops helping: a 70B with FP8 cache at 17K tokens of context tops out near 700 tokens/s per H100 at \(\eta = 0.6\). With 4-GPU replicas of 78 sequences each, a step takes about 36 ms of reads plus about 2 ms of scheduling and kernel launches, so a GPU makes about 520 tokens/s and each sequence moves forward at about 26 tokens/s.

4 · Little's law

\[\text{in flight} = \lambda \times T_{\text{traj}}\]

The number of trajectories alive at once equals the rate the trainer consumes them times how long each one lives. It sizes sandboxes, KV cache and connection pools. 8,192 trajectories per 13-minute step is \(\lambda \approx 10.6\) per second; at 11 minutes each, about 7,100 are alive at any moment.

5 · Weight-sync time

\[t_{\text{bcast}} \approx \frac{S}{b}\]
\[t_{\text{p2p}} \approx \max\!\Big(\frac{S\,R}{n\,b},\ \frac{S}{g\,b}\Big)\]

\(S\) is the model's bytes, \(b\) the per-GPU link (about 40 GB/s effective on 400 Gb/s), \(R\) the number of engine replicas, \(n\) the trainer GPUs sending and \(g\) the GPUs per replica receiving. A 70B in BF16 broadcasts in 3.5 s; in FP8, sharded across 4-GPU replicas, it moves in 0.44 s.

6 · Failures and checkpoints

\[\text{MTBF}_{\text{job}} \approx \frac{\text{MTBF}_{\text{GPU}}}{N}\]
\[\tau^{*} \approx \sqrt{2\,C\,\text{MTBF}_{\text{job}}}\]

At Llama 3's rate, one GPU runs about 2,100 days between interruptions, so 1,024 GPUs see one every two days and 16,384 one every three hours. \(C\) is how long a checkpoint blocks training; with asynchronous DCP it is about a second, so a 720-GPU trainer (MTBF about 70 hours) should checkpoint every 12 minutes, which in practice means every step. This is the Young–Daly interval.

The worked plan, in order

Coding agent: a 70B dense policy, 1,024 H100s, 1,024 tasks per step with 8 samples each, 25 turns of 500 generated and 700 tool tokens, 8 s of tool time per turn.

StepArithmeticResult
1 · Batch1,024 tasks × 8 samples; 2K prompt + 25 × (500 + 700) tokens8,192 trajectories of 32K tokens
2 · Trainer work8,192 × 32K = 262M tokens × 733 GFLOP ÷ (0.35 × 989 TFLOP/s)154 GPU-h per step
3 · Decode work8,192 × 12.5K = 102M tokens ÷ 516 tokens/s per GPU (4-GPU replicas, 78 sequences each)55 GPU-h
4 · Prefill work8,192 × 19.5K new tokens (prompt + tool output; earlier turns hit the prefix cache)10 GPU-h
5 · Split1,024 GPUs in proportion 65 : 154, rounded to whole replicas and nodes304 rollout + 720 trainer
6 · Step time154 GPU-h ÷ 720 GPUs ≈ 65 GPU-h ÷ 304 GPUs≈ 13 min
7 · Trajectory time25 × (500 tokens ÷ 26.5 tokens/s + 8 s tool); tail taken as 3× the mean11 min, tail 34 min
8 · Concurrency10.6 trajectories/s × 674 s; 2 vCPUs per sandbox7,100 sandboxes, 14,000 vCPUs
9 · Stalenesstrajectory time ÷ step time0.9 steps, 2.6 in the tail
10 · Sync and failures70.6B × 2 B ÷ 40 GB/s; 12 B × 70.6B checkpoint; 2,100 GPU-days ÷ 720 GPUs3.5 s sync, 847 GB, MTBF 70 h

Three conclusions fall out, and each is a design decision. The trainer is the bigger pool, because it processes 2.6 times more tokens than decode produces and does three to four passes over each, provided every turn finds the earlier turns in the prefix cache. If each turn re-prefilled its whole context, prefill would grow about twentyfold and rollouts would be the bigger pool, which is why §11 adds a CPU cache tier. Interviewers often expect rollouts to dominate, so say why they don't here and what that depends on. Rollouts still dominate wall-clock time in a synchronous loop, where a step takes 33 minutes and the GPUs are busy 43% of the time, so the loop must be asynchronous. (With all 1,024 GPUs generating, each replica holds only 32 sequences, which decode at about 46 tokens/s, so the slowest trajectory takes about 24 minutes; training adds 9 and switching roles 30 s.) And the system is a concurrency problem as much as a compute one: 7,100 live trajectories need sandboxes, KV cache and connection slots.

Table view

Memory-bound decode with each replica at its KV-cache limit, compute-bound prefill at 40% of FP8 peak, prefix caching across turns, pools split in proportion to their work and run asynchronously. The synchronous comparison runs every GPU through generation, then training, plus 30 s to switch roles; with every GPU generating, each replica holds fewer sequences, so each sequence decodes faster than in the split pools (about 46 against 26 tokens/s). Failure rate from Llama 3's 54-day report; checkpoint size 12 bytes per parameter.

Say it

“Each step is 8,192 trajectories of 32K tokens. The trainer pushes 262 million tokens through forward and backward, about 154 GPU-hours, and decode makes 102 million tokens at about 500 per GPU-second, about 65 GPU-hours with prefill. So I split 1,024 GPUs into roughly 300 for rollouts and 720 for training, which gives a 13-minute step. A trajectory lives about 11 minutes, so about 7,000 are in flight: that's my sandbox fleet, and it's why I'll run asynchronously.”

These constants are first-order. In a real design review, replace them in the first week: run a hundred trajectories, read tokens/s per GPU and the prefix-cache hit rate from vLLM's metrics, MFU from the trainer, and the tool-latency histogram from the sandboxes.
